doc.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022

title: How studio calls worked: Radio Registry and the Sinatra date
summary: Sessions were booked by answering service; Mike and Randy played on Sinatra's 'L.A. Is My Lady'.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Great. Thank you. We don’t have to spend a lot of time on this but can you describe what a typical studio session entailed? How do you get the phone call? How much do you know before you get there? And that kind of thing.

Well that’s a tough question to answer because there were — every one was so different. But how do you get the call — it was a lot less dramatic than you think although let me insert this story because it’s a good one. We were just talking about this record the other night. Mike and I played on a Frank Sinatra record called “L.A. is my Lady” — a whole

LP with Quincy Jones. It became pretty well known. There’s a short film out, I haven’t seen it in a long time, and Michael Jackson was planned to show up and they filmed the whole thing. And Mike and I were asked to do, they were going to put a long film out so a couple of guys came over to my apartment, Mike came over with a film crew and one of the questions was how did he get the call? And Mike made up a scenario, well we had gotten a call from — what was that club, I can’t think — Juli — Frank’s guy in New York, I can’t think of his name right now but he had a club under his name. We went over to the club and Frank was there and he said, “Come on guys, take a ride with me in the limo around Central Park I have a new project I want to tell you about.” And Mike went into a whole thing, it was all bullshit. Because the real way we got called was there was an answering service who called our answering machine. It was called Radio Registry. You might have heard of it. And that’s how 95% of the dates were booked. It was so busy you’d get a call, “Hello? This is Radio Registry are you available 10 ‘til 5 or 10 to 1 usually — 2 to 5 tomorrow it’s for so-and-so or they might mention the artist or the producer, plus an hour overtime if it was a commercial — 10 to 11 with a possible 20 it’s for Coca Cola. And you’d go, “Oh Coca Cola, yeah.” You never knew. But that’s how it worked. It wasn’t anywhere near as dramatic as probably people think. Every once in a while there were a couple of other contractors that would call, Sephra Herman — she would call personally sometimes. But that’s how we got the call from Frank.
How long did they wait before you called back before they go all right we’ve got to move on down the line to the next person?

Well they would wait, but you know you were trained, you would check your answer machine or when they had those things you wore on your belt to buzz when they would call. So you would make sure you call them every three or four hours when we were busy. And to further answer your question [inaudible] got called the day before the session. It was that last minute, because people procrastinate, you know writing. So more often than not you really had trouble planning your week because you never were sure when you were going to get a call.
